results.claim: The arbitrary-sharing-number no-teleport problem belongs to NP.
results.proof_sketch: Let L be the total number of feature occurrences. Every legal no-teleport transition has distinct endpoint tiles with a common live feature and therefore deletes at least those two occurrences. Thus every play has at most floor(L/2) transitions. A certificate is a starting tile followed by that polynomial-length tile sequence. A verifier tracks live occurrences, checks distinct consecutive tiles and a nonempty live intersection, deletes every feature live at both endpoints, and finally checks that no occurrence remains, all in polynomial time. Also, an unordered tile pair cannot recur: its first use deletes every then-live common feature, and deleted occurrences never become live again.

results.claim: There is an exact characterization by perfect matchings plus an ordered Euler trail with precedence constraints.
results.proof_sketch: For each feature f with support S_f, choose a perfect matching M_f, and let H be the simple set union of the M_f. A shared matching edge appears once in H because one transition simultaneously deletes every live feature common to its endpoints. Write m_f(v) for v's matching edge. The characterization requires an Euler-trail order tau of H such that for every e=uv in H\M_f with u,v in S_f, either m_f(u) precedes e or m_f(v) precedes e. Necessity follows from any play: f-deletions pair S_f, every move deletes some feature, no tile pair recurs, and a nonmatching f-edge can occur only after f has disappeared at an endpoint. For sufficiency, suppose the earliest matching event m_f(u) that should delete f fails because u lost f on an earlier nonmatching edge uw. Since m_f(u) is later, precedence forces m_f(w) before uw. By earliestness, m_f(w) successfully deleted f at w, so uw could not have deleted f at u, a contradiction. Hence all matching events succeed. Every H-edge belongs to some matching, so every transition is legal, and all occurrences are deleted. The featureless case uses the empty trail.

results.claim: If every occurring feature appears on exactly two tiles, no-teleport solvability is decidable in linear time even with unbounded sharing number.
results.proof_sketch: Build a simple graph K on edge-bearing tiles, with edge uv when at least one feature has support {u,v}. Such a feature can be deleted only by transition uv, and all features with the same endpoint pair remain synchronized and are deleted together; hence their shared edge has multiplicity one in K. A solution is therefore exactly an Euler trail using every edge of K. The featureless instance is trivially solved; otherwise the criterion is connectivity of the edge-bearing vertices and zero or two odd degrees. In the standard word-RAM model with array-indexed feature and tile identifiers, scan the L occurrences to obtain endpoint pairs, radix-sort the word-sized integer pairs, deduplicate them, and test connectivity and degree parity, all in deterministic O(L) time. The number of features sharing one pair is unrestricted.

results.claim: The obvious static relaxation—choosing feature-perfect-matchings whose simple union is Eulerian—is not sufficient.
results.proof_sketch: Take tiles 0,1,2,3,4 and feature supports {0,1}, {0,2}, {1,2}, {0,1,2,3}, and {0,1,2,4}. The first three force the core triangle. Tiles 3 and 4 each contain only their respective four-support feature, so they are the endpoints of any no-teleport play. If their incident edges attach to core vertices i and j, Euler parity forces i=j. Starting at 3, the play takes 3i, traverses the triangle as a circuit based at i, and ends with i4. Before the first triangle edge from i, the feature on {0,1,2,4} is live at every core tile; that edge deletes its occurrence at i, so the final i4 move is illegal. Reversing exchanges the two four-support features and gives the same contradiction. Yet choose matchings 03+12 and 04+12 for those features, with forced matchings 01, 02, and 12. Their simple union is {01,02,12,03,04}, connected with exactly odd vertices 3 and 4. The shared edge 12 is intentionally counted once. Thus an Eulerian simple union alone is insufficient.

results.claim: An exact state-space algorithm runs in O(n^2 L·2^L) time and O(n·2^L) space.
results.proof_sketch: Represent the live feature occurrences by an L-bit mask and memoize (current tile, live mask), giving at most n times 2^L states. From each state inspect the n-1 other tiles. A direct scan of the incidence data in O(L) time finds all features live at both endpoints; the transition is allowed exactly when this set is nonempty, and its two endpoint occurrences for every such feature are cleared. Each transition strictly lowers the live-occurrence count, so the recurrence is acyclic and exact. Trying every starting tile shares the memo table. Thus the time is O(n^2 L times 2^L), and a directly indexed memo table uses O(n times 2^L) space, apart from lower-order input and recursion storage.

final_writeup:
Resolution: PARTIAL. The target asks for a complete complexity classification at arbitrary sharing number: either a polynomial-time algorithm for all instances or a matching hardness result. Neither is proved here, so the open target is not claimed solved. The five verified claims below are nevertheless material partial progress.

Let S_f be the tile support of feature f. In any no-teleport play, the transitions that delete f pair the vertices of S_f, giving a perfect matching M_f. No unordered tile pair can be used twice, and each move deletes at least one feature, so the whole play is an Euler trail of the simple union H of these matchings. The word simple is essential: if several M_f share uv, the one transition uv deletes all corresponding live features simultaneously; it is not several parallel moves. This explicitly handles the applicable shared-edge warnings from the BugBank receipt.

Static matchings and Euler parity do not capture when occurrences disappear. The exact temporal condition is: for every edge e=uv of H that is not in M_f but has both endpoints in S_f, at least one of m_f(u),m_f(v) must precede e in the Euler order. Necessity is immediate from the deletion semantics. Sufficiency follows by the earliest-failure argument in the second proof sketch: an allegedly premature nonmatching deletion forces an earlier successful matching deletion at its other endpoint, making that premature deletion impossible. Thus the condition is an exact characterization, not merely a relaxation.

The five-tile instance with supports {0,1}, {0,2}, {1,2}, {0,1,2,3}, and {0,1,2,4} separates the static and temporal conditions. Its displayed matching union is the triangle 012 with leaves 3 and 4 both attached to 0, so it has an Euler trail. But any actual play must enter the triangle from one leaf, traverse it as a circuit, and leave through the other leaf. The first triangle move deletes at the attachment tile the feature needed for the final leaf move. Hence no no-teleport solution exists.

A broad special case does collapse to an ordinary Euler test. If every feature occurs twice, its only possible deleting transition is fixed. Collapsing all features with the same endpoint pair gives a simple graph K, and solutions are exactly Euler trails of K. This is deterministically linear in L on the standard word-RAM representation by radix-sorting endpoint pairs, deduplicating, and checking connectivity and parity; pairwise sharing itself may be unbounded.

For general instances, NP membership follows from the floor(L/2) move bound. Exact reachability is also decidable by memoizing the current tile and the L-bit live-occurrence mask, yielding O(n^2 L times 2^L) time and O(n times 2^L) space. These results expose the unresolved issue precisely: whether the matching choices plus their ordering constraints admit a polynomial algorithm or encode an NP-hard problem.
